normalized_decision.output: Analysis of the queue incident spanning 09:00 to 09:35 reveals a clear causal chain initiated by an external dependency rate-limiting event and amplified by an aggressive retry policy. At baseline (09:00), the system operated with queue depth at 120 and eight workers, which was apparently stable. Between 09:00 and 09:10, queue depth surged fifteen-fold to 1,850 while worker count remained constant, indicating an external trigger rather than a processing-side change. By 09:12, median task latency had increased nearly eightfold from 1.8 to 14.2 seconds, consistent with tasks stalling on outbound calls. At 09:14, system resource utilization remained modest (CPU 43%, memory 51%, disk 22%), ruling out local compute exhaustion as the bottleneck. At 09:15, dependency B was observed returning HTTP 429 responses for 31% of requests, establishing the upstream constraint. By 09:16, retry volume had escalated 420% using exponential backoff capped at three retries, meaning each rate-limited request could generate up to four total attempts, dramatically multiplying effective demand against an already saturated endpoint. The attempted remediation at 09:20 of doubling workers from 8 to 16 yielded only a 6% queue reduction over ten minutes, confirming that additional processing parallelism could not overcome the upstream rate limit — workers simply queued behind the same 429 wall. At 09:26, disabling retries for dependency B produced a 38% queue depth reduction in six minutes, directly demonstrating that retry amplification was a major contributor to queue growth, though at the cost of elevated direct failure rates. The incident resolved at 09:35 when dependency B's rate limits were raised, causing 429 responses to drop below 1% and queue depth to normalize below 150 within eleven minutes. E10 confirms no internal changes (deploy, schema, host restart, network route, or credential rotation) occurred during the incident window, eliminating endogenous causes. The primary cause is dependency B's rate limiting. The dominant amplifier was the retry policy, which converted a 31% partial failure condition into a multi-fold demand multiplier against a constrained resource. Adding workers was ineffective because the bottleneck was external rate capacity, not local processing throughput — additional workers merely competed for the same limited upstream budget. The retry policy is architecturally unsound for 429 responses: 429 explicitly signals the caller to reduce demand, yet exponential retries increase it. Retries on 429 should be suppressed or aggressively throttled, distinct from retries on transient 5xx errors. Key uncertainties include why dependency B began rate limiting at that specific time (possibly a shared-tenant spike), the agreed rate limit thresholds, and whether connection pooling or request batching could reduce per-request overhead. A plausible alternative hypothesis is that organic inbound traffic to our service surged, but this is poorly supported by the low resource utilization at E04 and the absence of any deployment or configuration change at E10; such a surge would also have elevated CPU or memory, which did not occur. A staged remediation plan should begin with circuit-breaker insertion and 429-aware retry suppression, proceed to outbound rate limiting and adaptive backoff with jitter, and conclude with improved early-warning alerting and a formal rate-limit agreement with the dependency B provider.

data.executive_summary: A queue depth incident at 09:10 was triggered by dependency B returning HTTP 429 for 31% of requests. The system's retry policy amplified the problem, increasing retry volume by 420% and converting partial failures into queue saturation. Doubling workers from 8 to 16 reduced queue depth by only 6%, confirming the bottleneck was upstream rate limiting, not local processing capacity. Disabling retries produced a 38% queue reduction in six minutes, proving retry amplification was the dominant secondary factor. The incident resolved when dependency B raised rate limits. No internal changes (deploys, schema, restarts, network, or credentials) occurred during the window. Remediation should prioritize circuit-breaker insertion, 429-aware retry suppression, outbound rate limiting, and a formal rate-limit agreement with the dependency provider.

findings.claim: Dependency B rate limiting (HTTP 429 for 31% of requests at 09:15) is the primary root cause of the queue incident.
The exponential backoff retry policy amplified queue depth by increasing retry volume 420%, converting a 31% partial failure into a multi-fold demand multiplier against a constrained endpoint.
Adding workers from 8 to 16 produced only a 6% queue reduction because the bottleneck was upstream rate capacity, not local processing throughput.
System resource utilization (CPU 43%, memory 51%, disk 22%) was well below saturation, ruling out local compute exhaustion as a contributing factor.
No internal changes occurred during the incident window (08:00-10:00), eliminating deploys, schema changes, host restarts, network route changes, and credential rotations as potential causes.

Disabling retries for dependency B reduced queue depth by 38% in six minutes but increased direct failure rate, confirming retry amplification as a key secondary factor and demonstrating the tradeoff involved.

Raising dependency B rate limits at 09:35 caused 429 responses to fall below 1% and queue depth to normalize below 150 within eleven minutes, confirming external rate capacity as the binding constraint.
Queue depth surged from 120 to 1,850 in ten minutes (09:00-09:10) while worker count remained at 8, indicating a rapid external trigger rather than a gradual processing degradation.

risks: Dependency B rate limiting may recur during peak traffic or shared-tenant contention, re-triggering queue saturation.
The current retry policy is architecturally unsuited for 429 responses, which explicitly signal demand reduction rather than retry.
No circuit breaker exists for dependency B, allowing retry storms to propagate unchecked into queue depth.
Queue monitoring does not currently alert on rate-limit-induced saturation patterns early enough for intervention.
Dependency B represents a single point of failure; loss of its capacity directly halts downstream processing.
Absence of outbound rate limiting means any retry policy can multiply effective demand beyond upstream tolerances.
uncertainties: Why did dependency B begin rate limiting at 09:10 specifically — was it a shared-tenant event, a capacity change on their side, or an organic traffic shift?
What is the agreed or documented rate limit threshold for dependency B, and was our request volume approaching it before 09:00?
Are there other consumers of dependency B that may have contributed to the rate-limit trigger during this window?
What is the normal baseline queue depth under steady state, and did the 120 reading at 09:00 already reflect elevated load?
Could connection pooling, request batching, or payload optimization reduce per-request overhead against dependency B's rate limit?

recommendations.action: Implement a circuit breaker for dependency B that opens on sustained 429 responses and fast-fails requests instead of queuing them.
recommendations.rationale: Disabling retries at 09:26 produced a 38% queue reduction, proving that suppressing demand to the constrained endpoint is the highest-leverage intervention.

recommendations.action: Suppress retries on HTTP 429 responses entirely, or implement a very conservative retry budget (e.g., ≤5% of failed requests) with jitter.
recommendations.rationale: 429 explicitly signals demand reduction; retrying increases effective load against a saturated resource, as demonstrated by the 420% retry volume increase at E06.

recommendations.action: Implement outbound rate limiting or a token-bucket governor for requests to dependency B, capping requests per second regardless of retry policy.
recommendations.rationale: Even with circuit breaker and retry suppression, a hard outbound cap prevents accidental demand spikes from reaching dependency B.

recommendations.action: Add queue depth and 429-rate alerting with thresholds calibrated to trigger before saturation (e.g., alert at 429 rate > 10% or queue depth > 500).
recommendations.rationale: The queue was at 1,850 by 09:10; earlier alerting would have shortened the incident window.

recommendations.action: Establish a formal rate-limit agreement or capacity reservation with dependency B's provider, including documented SLAs and escalation paths.
recommendations.rationale: The root cause was an external rate limit; a contractual agreement ensures visibility into limits and faster remediation.

recommendations.action: Implement adaptive worker scaling that is aware of upstream rate limits — scale down workers when 429 rates are high rather than up.
recommendations.rationale: Scaling from 8 to 16 workers at 09:20 had no effect because more workers cannot overcome an upstream rate limit; scaling down would reduce contention.

alternatives.name: Organic inbound traffic surge
pros: Could explain rapid queue depth increase from 120 to 1,850
Does not require external dependency as root cause
cons: E04 shows CPU at 43%, memory at 51%, disk at 22% — resource utilization would be elevated under a traffic surge
E10 rules out any deploy or configuration change that would alter traffic patterns
The 31% 429 rate at E05 is more consistent with an upstream constraint than a downstream traffic spike

alternatives.name: Network latency or packet loss causing timeouts
pros: Timeouts could cause task stalls that increase queue depth
Could affect outbound calls to dependency B
cons: E05 explicitly identifies HTTP 429 responses, not timeouts or connection errors
Network issues would likely affect all outbound dependencies, not just dependency B
E10 rules out network route changes during the window

alternatives.name: Internal resource contention (memory leak, disk I/O, or thread exhaustion)
pros: Latency increase from 1.8s to 14.2s at E03 could suggest resource contention
Queue depth increase could be a symptom of processing slowdown
cons: E04 shows all resource metrics well below saturation (CPU 43%, memory 51%, disk 22%)
E07 shows adding workers did not help, which is inconsistent with a processing bottleneck
E08 shows disabling retries (not freeing resources) reduced queue depth, pointing to retry amplification over resource contention

alternatives.name: Credential or authentication failure causing cascading errors
pros: Auth failures could cause repeated failed requests and queue buildup
cons: E10 explicitly rules out credential rotation during the window
E05 identifies HTTP 429 (rate limit), not HTTP 401/403 (auth failure)
The incident resolved when rate limits were raised at E09, not when any credential was refreshed

evidence.observation: At 09:00, queue depth was 120 and worker count was 8.
At 09:10, queue depth rose to 1,850 while worker count remained 8.
At 09:12, median task latency rose from 1.8 seconds to 14.2 seconds.
At 09:14, CPU utilization averaged 43%, memory 51%, and disk utilization 22%.
At 09:15, outbound dependency B began returning HTTP 429 for 31% of requests.
At 09:16, retry volume increased by 420%, using exponential backoff with a maximum of three retries.
At 09:20, increasing worker count from 8 to 16 reduced queue depth only 6% over ten minutes.
At 09:26, temporarily disabling retries for dependency B caused queue depth to fall 38% in six minutes, while direct failure rate increased.
At 09:35, dependency B rate limits were raised and HTTP 429 responses fell below 1%; queue depth then returned below 150 within eleven minutes.
No deploy, schema change, host restart, network route change, or credential rotation occurred between 08:00 and 10:00.

edge_cases: If dependency B returns 429 intermittently (below alerting threshold), retry amplification may cause slow queue buildup that is not detected until saturation.
If the circuit breaker opens too aggressively, transient 429 bursts may cause unnecessary request failures even when the rate limit would self-resolve quickly.
If outbound rate limiting is set too low, it may throttle legitimate traffic below dependency B's actual capacity during non-incident periods.
If queue depth monitoring relies on aggregate metrics, per-worker queue imbalance may mask saturation in specific processing lanes.
If retry suppression is applied uniformly, legitimate transient errors (non-429) may be incorrectly suppressed, increasing failure rates unnecessarily.
If dependency B raises rate limits temporarily during an incident and then lowers them again, the system may re-enter saturation without the retry amplification signal being as visible.
